stories.headline: WHITE HOUSE CONTRADICTS IRAN DEAL DRAFT, OIL WHIPSAWS TO $91
stories.body: A draft U.S.-Iran framework circulated before the open, briefly sending WTI below $90 on Strait of Hormuz reopening optimism — then the White House rejected key terms, demanding Iran fully dismantle its enrichment capacity. Oil snapped back to $91, still down 3.2% on the day. At $91, crude is pricing roughly a 50% deal probability; a finalized agreement would push WTI toward $72–75 by Q4 2026.

stories.headline: DOW SETS NEW RECORD AT ~50,663 WHILE NASDAQ FLAT AS CHIP RALLY PAUSES
stories.body: The Dow Jones rose 201 points (+0.4%) to a new all-time high, lifted by oil-decline beneficiaries in consumer and industrial names. The S&P 500 and Nasdaq each gained just 0.1%, however, as semiconductor stocks retreated after leading the market's monthlong surge. The divergence illustrates the Dow's price-weighted construction: when high-priced chip stocks stall, the cap-weighted indexes barely move but the Dow can still rally on cheaper cyclicals.

stories.headline: SPACEX IPO NOW 16 DAYS OUT; INSTITUTIONAL BOOK REPORTED OVERSUBSCRIBED
stories.body: The June 12 Nasdaq debut of SpaceX (SPCX) is generating the most pre-IPO buzz since Aramco's 2019 listing. At a $1.75 trillion target valuation, SPCX would instantly rank among the ten most valuable publicly traded companies globally. Institutional allocation demand is reportedly oversubscribed; Starlink subscriber growth will be the key metric watched at debut for earnings visibility.

stories.headline: 10-YEAR YIELD EASES TO 4.48%, DXY SLIPS BELOW 99.1 AS RISK PREMIUM FADES
stories.body: The 10-year Treasury yield fell 3 bps to 4.48% and the DXY dollar index slipped to 99.1 as Iran deal optimism reduced the geopolitical risk premium embedded in both assets. Lower oil prices trim headline CPI expectations, giving the Fed marginally more flexibility. Markets still price one 25 bps cut by year-end — today's yield move was too small to shift that consensus, but sustained oil weakness could.

stories.headline: SPURS SURVIVE ELIMINATION GAME 5, FORCE GAME 6; KNICKS AWAIT IN FINALS
stories.body: San Antonio won Game 5 last night to keep their WCF run alive at 3-2 vs. Oklahoma City; Game 6 is Thursday May 28. Meanwhile, the New York Knicks swept Cleveland 4-0 in the ECF to reach the NBA Finals for the first time since 1999. The Finals tip off June 3 on ABC — the Knicks' opponent TBD after Game 6.

stories.headline: DERWIN JAMES SIGNS $75.6M EXTENSION AS OTA INJURIES HIT THE GIANTS
stories.body: Chargers safety Derwin James agreed to a 3-year, $75.6M contract extension making him the highest-paid safety in NFL history. Elsewhere in OTAs, the Giants lost projected starting DL Roy Robertson-Harris for the season to a torn Achilles, a blow to New York's rebuilt defensive line after Dexter Lawrence II was traded to Cincinnati in April.

stories.headline: LSU CLAIMS TOP PORTAL CLASS WITH LEAVITT, SEATON, UMANMIELEN AMONG 8 TOP-100 ADDS
stories.body: As the 2026 portal window closes, LSU leads every ranking with QB Sam Leavitt (Arizona State), OT Jordan Seaton (Colorado), and edge Princewill Umanmielen (Ole Miss) among eight top-100 additions under Lane Kiffin. Washington begins official visits June 5, targeting 4-star safety Jayden Walk-Green (Corona Centennial HS, CA) among others.

stories.headline: FLORIDA TOPS WAY-TOO-EARLY 2026-27 POLLS AS NBA EARLY-ENTRY DEADLINE CLOSES TODAY
stories.body: With today's NBA early-entry withdrawal deadline (May 27) finalizing college rosters, Florida sits No. 1 in early 2026-27 projections after retaining Thomas Haugh, Alex Condon, and Rueben Chinyelu — the same frontcourt that won a title two seasons ago. The 2026-27 championship game is set for Ford Field in Detroit on April 5, 2027.

deepDive.title: The Strait of Hormuz as a pricing mechanism — how Iran's return reshapes global crude
content: Today's sharpest market move wasn't in equities — it was crude oil, which briefly fell below $90 on hopes of a U.S.-Iran nuclear deal before snapping back to $91 when the White House rejected key terms. The Strait of Hormuz, the 21-mile-wide chokepoint between the Persian Gulf and the Gulf of Oman, sits at the center of this volatility. Understanding how dramatically Iranian re-entry would shift global supply requires understanding exactly how much volume moves through it, and what happens to that volume when Iran is constrained.

The Strait handles roughly 20–21 million barrels of oil per day — approximately 20% of global petroleum liquids. Iran's pre-sanctions production capacity was about 3.8 million bbl/day; under the current sanctions regime, actual exports run closer to 1.3–1.5 million bbl/day. The gap has been absorbed by Saudi Arabia, UAE, and Iraq quietly expanding output to compensate. A deal that lifts sanctions would allow Iran to ramp exports within 3–6 months, adding roughly 1.5–2 million bbl/day to global supply. That incremental volume is equivalent to bringing a mid-tier OPEC producer from zero to full capacity — not a marginal adjustment, but a structural supply shift.

What most people miss is that the Iran story reshapes every other OPEC+ member's incentives simultaneously. When Iran was cut off, Saudi Arabia and the UAE captured market share and built leverage within the cartel. Bringing Iran back means they must either cut their own production to defend price, or accept a lower equilibrium — which strains cartel unity. The sharpest historical contrast is the September 2019 Abqaiq drone strike: a 5.7-million-bbl/day production disruption — roughly half of Saudi output — sent WTI up nearly 15% in a single session before recovering as spare capacity was deployed. Iran's return would apply comparable-magnitude downward pressure, but sustained over months rather than days, and with no offsetting demand shock to cushion it.

At today's WTI of $91, the market is embedding roughly a 50–60% deal probability, based on back-of-envelope math: Brent was around $95 before Iran talks began, and the market is pricing about half of the expected $8–10/barrel supply discount from Iranian re-entry. If a deal closes, most sell-side models cluster around $72–78 WTI equilibrium by Q4 2026. That lower-oil scenario matters well beyond energy stocks: a 1-million-bbl/day increase in Iranian supply historically reduces U.S. headline CPI by approximately 15–20 basis points over six months. Cheaper oil expands consumer purchasing power, reduces headline inflation, and gives the Fed more room to cut — which compresses discount rates and benefits rate-sensitive sectors like utilities, REITs, and long-duration technology.
